sections.title: Volume of 3D Shapes Made up of Cubes and Cuboids

learn.title: Volume
learn.html:
Volume is the space a solid takes up. We count it in unit cubes or in cm³ and m³.

A 1 cm cube has a volume of 1 cm³.

learn.title: Volume of a cube and a cuboid
learn.html:
Cube: length × length × length

Cuboid: length × width × height

Cube 2 cm by 2 cm by 2 cm: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm³

learn.title: Base area × height
learn.html:
The area of the bottom face is the base area (length × width).

Volume = base area × height, so height = volume ÷ base area.

learn.title: Edge of a cube
learn.html:
Face area known: which number × itself makes it? 36 = 6 × 6, so the edge is 6 cm.

Volume known: which number × itself × itself makes it? 125 = 5 × 5 × 5, so the edge is 5 cm.

learn.title: Solids made of cuboids
learn.html:
Split the solid into cuboids. Find each volume. Add them.

Or find a big cuboid and take away the missing part.

learn.title: Capacity
learn.html:
Capacity is how much a container can hold when full.

1 ℓ = 1,000 cm³ and 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³.

questions.label: Let's Recall 1 (a)
questions.q: The following solid is made up of unit cubes. Find the number of unit cubes and the volume of the solid.
questions.hint: Count layer by layer, or row by row. Don't forget cubes hidden at the back!
steps: The front has 3 columns and 2 rows, and it is 2 cubes deep: 3 × 2 × 2 = 12. On top at the left there are 2 more cubes: 12 + 2 = 14.
Each unit cube is 1 cubic unit, so the volume = 14 cubic units.
questions.why: The volume is the number of unit cubes.

questions.label: Let's Recall 1 (b)
questions.q: The following solid is made up of unit cubes. Find the number of unit cubes and the volume of the solid.
questions.hint: Count layer by layer, or row by row. Don't forget cubes hidden at the back!
steps: The left block is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. On top of it at the back are 2 more. The right block is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. 8 + 2 + 8 = 18.
Each unit cube is 1 cubic unit, so the volume = 18 cubic units.
questions.why: The volume is the number of unit cubes.

questions.label: Let's Recall 1 (c)
questions.q: The following solid is made up of unit cubes. Find the number of unit cubes and the volume of the solid.
questions.hint: Count layer by layer, or row by row. Don't forget cubes hidden at the back!
steps: It is a 4 by 4 square of cubes (16) with a 2 by 2 hole in the middle: 16 - 4 = 12.
Each unit cube is 1 cubic unit, so the volume = 12 cubic units.
questions.why: The volume is the number of unit cubes.

questions.label: Exercise 1 (a)
questions.q: Find the unknown edge of the cuboid. The volume of the cuboid is 2,100 m³ and the area of its shaded face is 700 m².

Height = volume ÷ area of shaded face = 2,100 ÷ 700
questions.why: Dividing the volume by the face area gives the third edge.

questions.label: Exercise 7
questions.q: From the given figure, add more cubes and/or cuboids to make the whole figure reach a volume of 424 cm³. (Answers vary.)
questions.hint: Find the volume you already have. How much more do you need?
steps: The given block: 5 × 4 × 10 = 200 cm³, minus the 3 × 3 × 4 hole = 36 cm³. So it is 164 cm³.
One way (the key's answer): a top bar 11 × 4 × 5 = 220 cm³ and a leg 2 × 4 × 5 = 40 cm³.
questions.answer: One answer: add an 11 × 4 × 5 cm bar and a 2 × 4 × 5 cm leg (260 cm³)
questions.why: Any extra pieces that add up to 260 cm³ work.

learn.title: Water in tanks
learn.html:
Volume of water = base area × water height.

Water height = volume ÷ base area.

learn.title: Emma pours water away
learn.html:
A tank is 38 cm × 24 cm, water 15 cm high. Emma pours away 5,472 cm³.

Drop in height = 5,472 ÷ (38 × 24) = 5,472 ÷ 912 = 6 cm

Water left = 15 - 6 = 9 cm high

learn.title: Litres and cm³
learn.html:
1 ℓ = 1,000 cm³ (× 1,000 to change ℓ into cm³).

1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³ = 1,000 ℓ.

learn.title: Draining a tank
learn.html:
Water drains at 16 ℓ a minute for 24 minutes: 16 × 24 = 384 ℓ = 384,000 cm³.

Tank 100 cm × 75 cm: height = 384,000 ÷ 7,500 = 51.2 cm

learn.title: Cube puzzles
learn.html:
Cube A has volume 27 cm³: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27, so its edge is 3 cm.

Cube B's edge is 4 times longer: 12 cm. Volume = 12 × 12 × 12 = 1,728 cm³.

questions.label: Exercise 10 (b)

Tank A and Tank B are rectangular tanks as shown below. At first, Tank A was completely filled with water and Tank B was empty. A tap was turned on to drain water from Tank A into Tank B at a rate of 10 ℓ per minute. When Tank B was completely filled with water, the height of the water level in Tank A became ⅔ of its original height.

learn.title: Unit 12 big ideas
learn.html:
Volume = length × width × height = base area × height.

Split solids into cuboids. 1 ℓ = 1,000 cm³. 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³.

learn.title: Pouring between tanks
learn.html: Water keeps its volume when it is poured. If 480 cm³ leaves a tank with base 480 cm², the water drops 1 cm. In a tank with base 640 cm², it rises 480 ÷ 640 = ¾ cm.

questions.label: Let's Think Along
questions.q: X and Y are two rectangular containers as shown below. The base area of X is 800 cm². The base area of Y is 600 cm². The height of X is ⅚ the height of Y. X contains water to a height of 36 cm. The volume of water in X will fill Y completely. How much more water is needed to fill X to the brim?
questions.hint: Find the water in X. That is Y's capacity, so you can find Y's height, then X's height.
steps: Water in X = 800 × 36 = 28,800 cm³. This fills Y, so Y holds 28,800 cm³.
Height of X = ⅚ of 48: 48 ÷ 6 = 8, 8 × 5 = 40 cm
questions.why: X holds 32,000 cm³ but has only 28,800 cm³.

questions.label: Problem Solving
questions.q: A and B are rectangular containers. The base area of A is 480 cm² and that of B is 640 cm². At first, A contained water to a height of 50 cm and B was empty. Peter poured some water from A into B. The height of the water level in A became twice that of B. What was the height of the water level in B?
questions.hint: Guess and check: when A drops 1 cm, B rises 480 ÷ 640 = ¾ cm.
steps: Every 1 cm drop in A pours 480 cm³ into B, which raises B by 480 ÷ 640 = ¾ cm.
Try a drop of 8 cm: A = 42 cm, B = 6 cm. 42 is 7 times 6. Too big.
Try a drop of 16 cm: A = 34 cm, B = 12 cm. Still more than twice.
Try a drop of 20 cm: A = 30 cm, B = ¾ × 20 = 15 cm. 30 is twice 15 ✓
So the water in B was 15 cm high.
questions.why: The water in A (30 cm) is twice the water in B (15 cm), and no water is lost.

questions.why: Volume ÷ (length × width) gives the height.
